newsitem.title: USA: Mich. court awards damages to schools in aid suit.
newsitem.headline: Mich. court awards damages to schools in aid suit.

text.p: Michigan Supreme Court justices have awarded damages estimated at $210 million to school districts challenging an old special education formula, the state's budget office spokeswoman said Monday.
Michigan officials also may consider resurrecting a proposed $1 billion school pension bond plan to pay the estimated damages from the 17-year-old case, budget spokeswoman Maureen McNulty said.
Supreme Court justices late Thursday ruled that the 84 school districts challenging the state's funding system were entitled to damages without interest for the school years 1991 to 1994.
While the justices set no specific amount, the damages for that period have been estimated at about $210 million, much less than the $492 million lower court judgment the state had appealed.
The districts that brought the lawsuit against the state were "delighted" by the decision even with the reduction from the state appeals court award, attorney Dennis Pollard said.
"The court had tough policy issues to consider," Pollard said. "This has taken 17 years, which is far too long for any litigant."
Pollard also said the state has not yet met its special education funding mandate.

Lawmakers in July rejected Treasurer Doug Roberts' pension bond plan, which would have required participating districts to drop any potential claims from the special education lawsuit, commonly referred to as Durant.

The plan would have fully funded the teacher retirement system and allowed employees the option of a pension or defined contribution plan, creating annual savings that could be used to cover the Durant decision, McNulty said.

"It's very good to have a final decision, we definitely know the parameters we have to work within now," McNulty said. "But it is still a significant fiscal responsibility we are looking at and we will have to look closely at the state budget in terms of paying it."

The justices found in a divided decision that districts "typically" would be limited to non-monetary relief in the future, but the state's "prolonged recalcitrance" required a damage award in this case.

Three justices dissented, contending that the Supreme Court had no authority to award monetary damages. By doing so, the Supreme Court has in effect compensated taxpayers by paying money to themselves, the dissenting justices found.
